Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) face a fundamental limitation:
. Even frontier models like GPT-5 experience significant performance degradation as input context grows longer. This happens because:
Attention mechanisms struggle to maintain focus across very long sequences
Important information gets "lost" when surrounded by large amounts of text
Models have hard context window limits (e.g., 272K tokens for GPT-5)
Performance degrades faster for more complex tasks
The fundamental insight of Recursive Language Models is elegantly simple:
treat the prompt as part of the external environment rather than feeding it directly into the neural network
Instead of forcing the entire prompt through the transformer's attention mechanism, RLMs store the prompt as a variable that the LLM can programmatically interact with using code.

By breaking large problems into smaller chunks and processing them with sub-LLM calls, RLMs avoid the context rot problem. Each sub-LLM sees a manageable context where it can maintain full attention.

The REPL environment maintains state across iterations. Results from sub-LLM calls can be stored in variables and combined later, enabling complex multi-step reasoning.
RLMs successfully handled inputs two orders of magnitude beyond model context windows
Outperformed base models and other scaffolds by up to 2x on long-context tasks
On OOLONG-Pairs (quadratic complexity), base models scored <0.1% while RLMs achieved 58%
Comparable or lower API costs than alternatives, with selective context viewing
Works with both closed (GPT-5) and open (Qwen3-Coder) models

Recursive Language Models represent a paradigm shift in how LLMs handle long contexts. By treating the prompt as an external environment rather than direct neural network input, RLMs enable LLMs to process arbitrarily long inputs through intelligent decomposition, selective access, and recursive sub-calls—all while maintaining strong performance and reasonable costs.
